cues.text: For this project, ask: could inadequate mixing within the intended batch
range lead to non-uniform product before transfer?
This is more useful than asking whether the vessel is risky.
The question identifies a possible failure, product consequence and
operating context.
Our diagram shows the possible chain from lost mixing to variable
concentration and a potentially affected dose.
It is not measured process data and does not prove that any real
vessel performs poorly.
A stopped agitator is a failure mode.
Non-uniform concentration may be a product-quality effect, depending on
the formulation and process.
An incorrect delivered dose may be a patient consequence.
These links require scientific understanding; they are not automatic for
every liquid.
The exercise asks you to explain the chain and list the evidence needed
to judge it.
Avoid assigning a score before you understand the scenario.
ICH Q9(R1) links risk decisions to scientific knowledge and
patient protection.
The degree of formality should reflect risk, uncertainty, importance and
complexity.
For our case, a small development study may not represent the full batch range.
Record that limitation and plan how to reduce uncertainty.
A low number based on a guess is not stronger evidence than a
clearly stated unknown.
Invite people who understand the process, equipment and potential consequences.
Ask each person which assumptions could be wrong and what evidence would
change the decision.
If the project deadline is influencing scores, make that bias explicit.
In the activity, write one risk question and one cause-to-harm chain.
Keep the language specific enough that another reviewer can disagree with
it constructively and identify what needs checking.
